patch.description:
Replace the command the container starts with, or send `null` to go back to the template's.

Exec form, the same as Docker's own `Cmd`: `["node", "index.js"]`. Each element is one argument and nothing is passed through a shell, so shell features need a shell asked for by name — `["bash", "-lc", "npm ci && node ."]`.

Only templates that leave the command to you accept this. A database or a game server is started by its image in a way the image owns — its ports, its config files and its backups all assume that entrypoint ran — so those refuse with `COMMAND_MANAGED` rather than accepting a value they would ignore. Runtime templates (Node, Python, Java, Go and the rest) are the ones this exists for.

**Takes effect on the next start.** The command is baked into the container when it is created, so a running app keeps the one it was created with — restart it to apply.

**Required API key permission:** `apps:write`

post.summary: Preview a start command
post.description:
Resolve a draft start command against the app's real environment, without saving or restarting anything.

`$NAME` and `${NAME}` are substituted from the same environment the container is created with — the template's variables, yours, and the app's own address. `$$` is a literal dollar sign. An argument is never re-split, so a value containing a space stays one argument, unlike a shell.

`available` is everything you may reference, which is what a dashboard builds its autocomplete from. `referenced` is what this draft actually used, with `defined: false` on anything nothing supplies — those expand to an empty string rather than failing, so this is where a typo becomes visible.

Values of variables the template marks secret are withheld: `value` is `null` and `secret` is true. They still substitute correctly in the container.

Send no `command` to preview what the app would start with as it stands.

**Required API key permission:** `apps:write`

post.summary: Create an app, paid from balance
post.description:
Provision an app on a node and charge the account balance for it: reserve its ports, create its ZFS volume with the plan's storage quota, create its private network and register its managed domain. This is the counterpart to `POST /apps/order`, which raises a transaction to be paid externally and builds nothing until it settles.

The app is created STOPPED — start it explicitly, so a creation that succeeds is never confused with a container that failed to boot. `hostname` is the only name you choose; the public domain is derived from it and is immutable. `version` pins one of the template's versions — omit it for the template default. Pinning is what protects a customer from a moving tag, since the tag itself is resolved fresh on every start.

**Required API key permission:** `apps:write`

post.summary: Run a command in the container
post.description:
Run a command inside the running container and wait for it to finish.

`GET /apps/{id}/terminal` reaches the same place interactively; this is the shape a script or an agent can use — argv in, output and exit code out, no session to hold open.

**Exec form.** `["ls", "-la", "/data"]` — each element is one argument and nothing goes through a shell, so `&&`, pipes and globs need a shell asked for by name: `["sh", "-lc", "ls /data | wc -l"]`.

This is `docker exec`, not the app's start command: nothing here changes how the container starts, and the process ends when the command does.

Bounded on both axes. Output stops at 1 MB and comes back with `truncated: true`; the call is abandoned after `timeoutMs` with `timedOut: true` and `exitCode: null`, which means the command may still be running inside the container. stdout and stderr are interleaved in the order the container produced them.

**Required API key permission:** `apps:write`

post.summary: Add a custom domain
post.description:
Point a domain you own at this app.

CNAME it at the app's managed hostname first — that record is what makes traffic arrive at all, so proving control costs no extra step. The target is returned as `verificationTarget`. A zone apex cannot hold a CNAME, so an A record resolving to the same addresses is accepted too.

The domain is created `pending` and is NOT routed until it verifies; routing on request would let anyone point a record at us and have the node answer for their hostname. Verification is re-checked every five minutes, and you can force a check with `POST /apps/{id}/exposures/{exposureId}/verify`.

Hostnames under `storiza.app` are refused — those are ours, and the app already has one.

post.summary: Add an SSH public key to the signed-in user's account
post.description:
Stores an SSH **public** key that can then be attached to any number of servers by passing `sshKeyId` when ordering a VPS. The key is parsed the way `ssh-keygen -l` parses it: the algorithm must be one OpenSSH still accepts, and the blob's own header must agree with the prefix. A mismatch is rejected here rather than by sshd on a machine you can no longer reach.

The trailing comment is kept for display but stripped from what gets installed. Adding the same key twice returns `409 SSH_KEY_DUPLICATE` -- keys are compared by fingerprint, not by text, so re-pasting with a different comment is still a duplicate.

Never send a private key.

**Required API key permission:** `account:write`

post.summary: Renew a VPS for another period now
post.description:
Pays for the next period of this server's subscription — or its backup add-on, with `target: "backup"` — without waiting for the automatic renewal.

The period and the price come from the subscription, so this buys exactly one more of what the server is already on. The only choice is how to pay for it.

Leave `method` out and it comes from the wallet, as the automatic renewal does, and nothing about the subscription changes. Name a provider's own rail instead — `whop_cards` — and the subscription **moves to that provider**: it is sold there as a recurring plan, that provider re-charges the saved card on its own schedule from then on, and our balance worker stops billing the row. Nobody is billed twice, because only one of them ever bills it.

Because the provider's schedule starts the day it is paid, moving is only allowed once the current period has run out — otherwise the days already paid for would be lost. Renewing early is a wallet-only operation and anything else returns `RENEWAL_WOULD_LOSE_TIME`.

Only subscriptions Storiza bills itself can be renewed here. One billed by an external provider renews on that provider's own schedule — charging it again from our side would take payment twice for the same days — so it returns `SUBSCRIPTION_EXTERNALLY_BILLED` and is managed with `POST /payments/subscriptions/:id/manage`.

Paid from the balance, settlement is immediate: the returned transaction is already `completed` and the period has moved. Paid any other way it comes back `pending` with a `checkoutUrl`, and the period moves when that payment settles — so treat the response as a transaction to follow, not as a renewal that happened.

Time is added, never reset — renewing early extends from the end of the period already paid for. Renewing after a lapse starts the new period at payment and brings a server that was powered off for non-payment back up.

**Required API key permission:** `vps:write`

post.description:
Charges the difference between the current plan and the new one for the days remaining in the current period, then resizes the machine and re-prices future renewals.

get.summary: List the VPS plan categories with their hardware and datacenters
get.description:
Lists the visible VPS plan categories, highest priority first. Each carries its hardware `specifications`, the datacenter names its plans can be built in (`supportedDatacenters`) and whether it still takes new orders (`allowNewOrders` — a category that does not only renews existing servers). Plans link to a category through `categoryId`. Pass `includeHidden=true` to include hidden categories. Supports the standard filtering query parameters (`_page`, `_limit`, `_search`, `_sort_by`).

**No API key needed** — this endpoint is public.

get.summary: List VPS creation templates configurations
get.description:
Returns every VPS OS template in one response, ordered by `sortOrder`. There is no pagination and no filtering: the catalogue is small and the creation wizard needs all of it at once, so it is fetched once and narrowed in the client.

`instructions` is left out -- it is a long per-template document that would dominate the payload; read it from the template's own page.

**No API key needed** — this endpoint is public.
